summary: Famine drives ten of Jacob's sons to Egypt, where Joseph recognizes them, accuses them of spying, detains Simeon, and requires Benjamin's return. Jacob eventually entrusts Benjamin to Judah as hunger worsens; Joseph welcomes the brothers with a feast, then orders his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack to test their intentions toward one another.
whyItMatters: Food scarcity brings the divided family into Joseph's power and tests whether the brothers will protect the youngest son. Jacob's grief and the hidden money make the journey emotionally fraught before the cup is planted.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: Famine-stricken Canaan, Egypt's grain stores, and Joseph's household across the brothers' two journeys.
context.literaryForm: Famine and recognition narrative with detention, family negotiation, a banquet, and a planned test.

before.text: The seven plentiful years have ended. The famine Joseph predicted now reaches Canaan and forces Jacob's household to seek Egyptian food.

here.text: The brothers do not recognize the official who controls their food, while Joseph uses Benjamin's presence to examine whether their relationships have changed.

after.text: The planted cup is discovered, and Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place before Joseph reveals his identity.

outline.heading: Stored food in a barren world
outline.note: Egypt’s reserves attract buyers, including ten sons of Jacob.

outline.heading: Recognition, detention, and returned money
outline.note: Joseph keeps Simeon and demands the youngest brother while secretly restoring the payment.

outline.heading: Jacob refuses another risk
outline.note: The report and unexplained money intensify his fear of losing Benjamin.

outline.heading: Hunger forces a new decision
outline.note: As famine worsens, Jacob rejects Reuben’s pledge and accepts Judah’s responsibility.

outline.heading: The brothers welcomed and tested
outline.note: Simeon is released, Benjamin receives special attention, and Joseph orders the cup planted.

keyVerses.text: And Jacob said: 'Me have ye bereaved of my children! Joseph is not and Simeon also is not, and ye will take Benjamin away. On me has your wickedness come.
keyVerses.why: Jacob’s response makes the accumulated losses and fear behind his refusal explicit.

keyVerses.text: And Judah came near and said: 'Send him with me, and if I do not bring him back to thee, let me bear the blame before thee all the days of my life.'
keyVerses.why: Judah offers enduring personal responsibility for Benjamin’s safe return.

keyVerses.text: And Joseph devised a plan whereby he might learn their thoughts as to whether thoughts of peace prevailed amongst them, and he said to the steward who was over his house: 'Fill all their sacks with food, and return their money unto them into their vessels, and my cup, the silver cup out of which I drink, put it in the sack of the youngest, and send them away.'
keyVerses.why: The narrator states the purpose of Joseph’s plan: to learn whether the brothers intend peace.

questions.question: Why is Egypt able to supply food?
questions.answer: Joseph preserved grain during the plentiful years and now opens the stores to sell it. The chapter also says many Egyptians copied his storage practice and fed themselves from their own reserves during the first famine year.

questions.question: Why does Joseph accuse his brothers of spying?
questions.answer: He recognizes them while they do not recognize him, but he does not reveal his identity. This chapter records the accusation, detention, and demand for Benjamin without explicitly explaining each of those early actions as a separate test.

questions.question: What does being put “in ward” mean?
questions.answer: It means being held in custody. Joseph initially detains the group, then keeps Simeon while sending the other nine back with food.

questions.question: Why does the returned money alarm Jacob?
questions.answer: He hears that Simeon is held and that Benjamin must travel, then sees that the payment has mysteriously returned in each sack. The narrator explicitly connects that unexplained return with his fear of sending Benjamin.

questions.question: What is wrong with Reuben’s offered guarantee?
questions.answer: He offers the lives of his two sons if Benjamin does not return, making uninvolved children answer for a failed promise. Jacob refuses; the narrative reports the offer without requiring readers to treat that threatened substitution as acceptable.

questions.question: How does Judah’s promise differ?
questions.answer: Judah offers to bear the blame himself for the rest of his life if he fails to bring Benjamin back. Jacob then sends Benjamin, and Judah's personal responsibility becomes crucial in the next chapter.

questions.question: Does the final verse endorse every method Joseph uses?
questions.answer: It explains that he wants to know whether peaceful intentions prevail among the brothers, but the method is to plant evidence against Benjamin. A stated goal does not remove the coercion and danger created by the deception.

glossary.def: Custody or detention, first imposed on the brothers together and then on Simeon alone.
The household officer instructed by Joseph to fill the sacks and hide the silver cup.
The places where grain from the abundant years has been preserved for the famine.
